sample:
10 units, each with worked examples, a 10-mark practice task, common mistakes and quick recall

How this book matches your exam. Research check: Cambridge IGCSE First Language English 0500 has Paper 1 Reading (2 hours, 80 marks, 50%) plus either Paper 2 Directed Writing and Composition or the Coursework Portfolio. The Reading paper changes for exams from 2027:

  • Exams up to 2026: three questions. Q1 is comprehension of Text A (15 marks) and a summary of Text B (15). Q2 is short answers (10) and a language task (15) on Text C. Q3 is an extended response (25).
  • Exams from 2027: four 20-mark questions. Q1 is comprehension of Text A. Q2(a) is a summary of Text B, and Q2(b) is a new 5-mark attitude question. Q3 is short answers and language analysis on Text C. Q4 is an extended response.

Both versions test the same reading skills:

  • R1: explicit meaning.
  • R2: implicit meaning and attitudes.
  • R3: analysing, evaluating and developing ideas.
  • R4: how writers achieve effects.
  • R5: selecting information for a purpose.

This book trains R1, R2, R3 and R5. Book 2 covers the summary and Book 3 covers writers' effects. All extracts are original and written for practice. The marking guides are our own, not official Cambridge mark schemes.

Unit 1 of 10: How the Reading Paper Works

Key ideas

  • You get three texts (about 1,400 words in total from 2027; Text A and B are about 700–750 words each up to 2026). Spend about 15 minutes reading before you write.
  • Marks guide length. A 1-mark question needs one precise point; a 3-mark question needs three separate points.
  • Command words: identify or give (find it), explain (say what it means or why), using your own words (do not copy), how does the writer... (methods and effects).
  • Answer from the text, not from your own opinion. Every point must be traceable to a line.
  • No dictionary is allowed, so work out difficult words from context.

Worked examples

Example 1: matching length to marks. "Give two reasons why the village was abandoned. [2]" needs two short, separate reasons, not a paragraph.

Example 2: tracking the line. Questions on Text A usually follow the order of the text, so the answer to question (c) is usually after the answer to (b).

Example 3: a time plan (2027 format, 4 × 20 marks). Reading 15 minutes, then about 25 minutes per question, leaving 5 minutes to check.

10-mark practice task

Extract (original): "The ferry left at dawn, but by then most of the island was already awake. Fishermen untangled nets on the jetty, the bakery window glowed, and old Mrs Darko was sweeping the same three steps she had swept every morning for forty years. Visitors called the island 'sleepy'. They had never been there at five in the morning."

(a) When did the ferry leave? [1]

(b) Name three activities happening on the island early in the morning. [3]

(c) What does "the same three steps she had swept every morning for forty years" suggest about Mrs Darko? [2]

(d) Explain why the writer disagrees with visitors who call the island "sleepy". [2]

(e) What is the effect of the final short sentence? [2]

Answers: (a) At dawn. (b) Fishermen untangling nets; the bakery working (window glowing); Mrs Darko sweeping her steps. (c) She keeps the same routine, showing she is dedicated, traditional or set in her habits (1 mark each for two ideas). (d) The island is busy before visitors are awake (1); visitors only see it later, so they misjudge it (1). (e) It is blunt and slightly humorous (1) and corrects the visitors' view, making the writer sound knowing (1).

Marking guide (our own): one mark per valid point as shown.

Common mistakes

  1. Writing long paragraphs for 1-mark questions. 2. Using your own knowledge instead of the text. 3. Skipping the 15 minutes of reading. 4. Ignoring the mark allocation. 5. Answering about the wrong paragraph.

Quick recall

  1. How many marks is the Reading paper? 2. What does R2 test? 3. What does "using your own words" mean? 4. How should you use the number of marks? 5. Can you use a dictionary?

Answers: 1) 80. 2) Implicit meanings and attitudes. 3) Rephrase; do not copy key words. 4) As the number of separate points needed. 5) No.
